chapter.name: India, That Is Bharat
chapter.blurb: India has had many names across its long history, reflecting shifting borders and different peoples describing the land. Its own inhabitants used names such as 'Sapta Sindhava' (Rig Veda, for the northwest), 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Jambudvipa' (Mahabharata, and later Ashoka's inscriptions, for the whole Subcontinent), and eventually 'Bharata' (Vishnu Purana, Tamil poetry, and the Constitution's 'India, that is Bharat'). Foreign visitors and invaders, building on 'Sindhu' (the Indus River), gave rise to 'Hindu' (Persian), 'Indoi'/'Indike' (Greek, source of 'India'/'Inde'), 'Yintu'/'Yindu'/'Tianzhu' (Chinese), and 'Hindustan' (first in a Persian inscription).

scope_in.item: Introduction: India's shifting borders and names across history; the 'Indian Subcontinent' as a broader historical term; sources for learning about the past (ancient texts, travellers'/pilgrims' accounts, inscriptions)
'Sapta Sindhava' -- the Rig Veda's name for the northwest of the Subcontinent ('land of the seven rivers'), from 'Sindhu' (the Indus River, or a river in general)

Regions named in the Mahabharata's running text (Kashmira, Kurukshetra, Vanga, Pragjyotisha, Kaccha, Kerala) and their rough modern equivalents; 'Bharatavarsha' and 'Jambudvipa' as Mahabharata-era names for the whole Subcontinent; Ashoka's inscription (~250 BCE) using 'Jambudvipa' for all of India plus parts of Bangladesh, Pakistan and Afghanistan

'Bharata' becoming the common name for the Subcontinent: the Vishnu Purana's definition (north of the ocean, south of the snowy mountains), the ancient Tamil poem describing similar boundaries, the north ('Bharat') and south ('Bharatam') forms, and the Constitution's opening phrase 'India, that is Bharat' / 'Bharat arthath India'

How foreigners named India via the Persian-Greek route: Persian 'Hind'/'Hidu'/'Hindu' (from 'Sindhu', a purely geographical term in ancient Persian), Greek 'Indoi'/'Indike' (dropping the 'h' absent in Greek), and English 'India'/French 'Inde' as descendants

How foreigners named India via the Chinese route ('Yintu'/'Yindu', and 'Tianzhu' meaning also 'heavenly master'), the term 'Hindustan' (first in a Persian inscription, later used by invaders of India), the monk Xuanzang's 7th-century CE journey, and the chapter's closing summary of all the names covered

scope_out.item: Exact modern-day identifications of the Mahabharata regions shown only on the map (Fig. 5.4), e.g. Kamboja, Gandhara, Druhyu, Kaikeya, Madra, Sauvira, Vahlika, Shivi, Matsya, Anarta, Avanti, Mahishmati, Vidarbha, Ashmaka, Kishkindhya, Chola, Pandya, Chedi, Kashi, Karusha, Dakshina Kosala, Pundra, Videha, Kosala, Magadha, Anga, Suhma, Kalinga, Shurasena, Panchala, Ambastha, Dravida, Surashtra
scope_out.reason: The chapter's own caption for Fig. 5.4 explicitly says 'You do not need to remember those regions'; only the regions named in the running text (Kashmira, Kurukshetra, Vanga, Pragjyotisha, Kaccha, Kerala) are in scope.

scope_out.item: The named rivers on the physical map of the Indian Subcontinent (Fig. 5.2), e.g. Indus, Ravi, Sutlej, Sarasvati, Ganga, Chambal, Narmada, Brahmaputra, Mahanadi, Kaveri, Godavari, Krishna, Tapti, Yamuna, Beas, Jhelum, Chenab
scope_out.reason: The map is an orienting illustration for the chapter's naming discussion, not a river-geography lesson; only 'Sindhu'/the Indus, which the naming chain depends on, is in scope.

scope_out.item: The content of the Indian Constitution beyond the opening phrase 'India, that is Bharat' / 'Bharat arthath India'
scope_out.reason: The chapter's own margin note says the Constitution 'will be studied in Grade 7'; this chapter uses only its opening naming phrase.

scope_out.item: The open 'LET'S EXPLORE' table-completion activity of names by language (blank Persian/Greek/Chinese/Arabic columns) and the open map-recognition activity for Fig. 5.4
scope_out.reason: Open, worksheet-style class activities with no single fixed textual answer beyond facts already covered elsewhere in the running text.

scope_out.item: Later historical use of 'Hindustan' under Mughal or British rule, and any general political history of those periods
scope_out.reason: The chapter stops at the term's first appearance in a Persian inscription about 1,800 years ago and its later adoption by 'most invaders of India'; it does not narrate Mughal or British-period history.

scope_out.item: The doctrinal or textual content of the Buddhist manuscripts Xuanzang collected and translated
scope_out.reason: The chapter's 'Don't Miss Out' aside gives only his travel dates, purpose and duration (7th century CE, 17 years, Sanskrit to Chinese translation), not the content of the texts themselves.

concepts.name: India's shifting boundaries and how we learn about its past
concepts.description: Today's India is a modern nation with defined borders, but the region -- often called the 'Indian Subcontinent' -- looked very different 500, 2,000 and 5,000 years ago, and has been known by many names; we learn about this past from ancient texts, travellers'/pilgrims' accounts, and inscriptions.
concepts.idea: India's borders and name have changed greatly across history; the region is often called the 'Indian Subcontinent' in this broader historical sense.
concepts.rule: We learn about India's past and evolution from many different sources: ancient texts, the accounts of travellers and pilgrims, and inscriptions.
concepts.example: The chapter opens with Sri Aurobindo's quotation about a 'spiritual and cultural unity' among the peoples living 'between the Himalayas and the two seas'.

questions.a: India is called an ancient land with many names because the region has existed and been inhabited for thousands of years, and in that time different groups of people -- both its own inhabitants and visitors from outside -- gave it different names, so no single name has been used throughout its whole history.

questions.q: A friend tells you, 'Since India today has one official name, it probably always had just one name.' Using at least two ideas from this chapter, write a short response explaining whether your friend is right or wrong.
questions.a: My friend is wrong. questions.q: The chapter opens with a quotation from Sri Aurobindo about a 'spiritual and cultural unity' among the peoples 'between the Himalayas and the two seas.' Analyse what this suggests about how the chapter wants you to think about India's identity, beyond just its name.
questions.a: It suggests that the chapter sees India's identity as resting not only on the specific name used at a given time, but also on an underlying spiritual and cultural unity shared by the peoples living across the wide geographical region bounded by the Himalayas and the two seas (the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal), which has persisted even as names and political borders changed.
s: Notes that the quotation points to a shared spiritual/cultural unity rather than just a name
Connects this to the region between the Himalayas and the two seas persisting despite changing names/borders

questions.q: Do you think it is important for a country to know the many different names it has been called through history? Give reasons for your view, using the chapter's introduction to support your answer.
questions.a: Answers will vary; a good answer might argue it is important because it helps a country understand its long and shared past, connect with the many peoples who have lived there and named it, and appreciate the deep cultural roots behind ideas like 'Bharata', while also acknowledging that too much focus on old names could distract from present-day identity; reasons should be tied to the chapter's point that we learn about the past through varied evidence such as texts, travel accounts and inscriptions.
s: Gives a clear opinion (yes/no/partly) with at least one reason
Reason is grounded in the chapter's idea that many sources reveal many past names
Answer shows balanced thinking, e.g. considering a counterpoint or limitation

To ask what India was called is really to ask who has known this land, and how.' (Any well-reasoned original opening in a similar spirit should be credited.)
s: Sentences meaningfully introduce the theme of India having many historical names
Draws on the chapter's substance (sources, or at least one historical name)

questions.q: Using the chapter, explain the chain of reasoning by which the modern English word 'India' and the ancient term 'Sapta Sindhava' are ultimately connected.
questions.a: Both terms trace back to the same root word, 'Sindhu' (a name for the Indus River). The Rig Veda used 'Sindhava' (from 'Sindhu') to form 'Sapta Sindhava' for the northwest region. Later, Persians adapted 'Sindhu' into 'Hindu'/'Hind'/'Hidu'; the Greeks, dropping the 'h' sound they lacked, turned this into 'Indoi'/'Indike', which eventually gave English 'India'. So 'Sapta Sindhava' and 'India' share the same ultimate root, 'Sindhu', even though they came into use through very different routes and refer to different extents of territory.
s: Identifies 'Sindhu' as the shared root behind both terms
Traces the Persian/Greek adaptation chain from Sindhu to Hindu to Indoi/India
Notes that despite the shared root, the two terms originally covered different extents of territory

questions.a: 'Sapta Sindhava' is an earlier name, used in the Rig Veda, India's most ancient text, and it covers only the northwest region (the land of the seven rivers). questions.q: Do you think a name like 'Sapta Sindhava', which describes a place by its rivers, is a good way to name a region? Give your view with reasons, considering both its usefulness and its limitations.
questions.a: Answers will vary. A good answer might say such a name is useful because rivers are a stable, easily recognisable geographic feature that people living in the region would immediately understand, and it reflects the real importance of rivers for water, farming and travel. A limitation is that it only covers one region (the northwest) and cannot describe the entire Subcontinent, and it says nothing about the people, culture or political organisation of the region, unlike names such as 'Bharatavarsha'.
s: Gives a clear view with at least one reason it is useful
Gives at least one limitation of a river-based regional name
Reasoning is grounded in details from the chapter (e.g. contrast with whole-Subcontinent names)

questions.a: Answers will vary widely and should be judged on reasoning rather than a fixed answer; for example, a student might propose combining a number of major local rivers with a word meaning 'river' or 'land', explaining that just as 'Sapta Sindhava' used 'sapta' (seven) and 'sindhava' (of rivers) to describe the northwest by its rivers, their own name should describe their region the same way -- by naming or counting its rivers.
s: Proposes an original name following a similar naming logic (number + river-word)
Explains the reasoning by explicit reference to how 'Sapta Sindhava' was formed
Name and explanation are internally consistent with each other
